card.name: Vayia Strose kai Louloudia
card.tagline: A Samian line dance weaving dual files into a single circle for Apokries.
card.profile: Vayia Strose kai Louloudia is a Greek folk dance from the island of Samos performed during Apokries (Carnival) and at social gatherings. Stylistically similar to the Syrtos, the dance features a distinctive spatial transition where participants form two lines within a circle, collapse into a single line, and expand back out into two lines at designated intervals of the song. Its title—meaning 'lay bay leaves and flowers'—stems from verses authored by the Samian poet Sideris Zisimou.
card.insight: Danced on the Greek island of Samos during Carnival, Vayia Strose kai Louloudia takes its name from a lyric by Samian poet Sideris Zisimou and features dancers shifting between two concentric lines and one.
card.profile_long:
Vayia Strose kai Louloudia originates from the island of Samos in Greece, taking its name from a phrase meaning 'lay bay leaves and flowers'. The dance's name is derived from the works of Samian poet Sideris Zisimou. Historically tied to the island's seasonal celebrations, it serves as a central feature of Apokries (Carnival) as well as general social gatherings, maintaining communal bonds through shared song and step.

In execution, the dance is closely aligned with the broader Syrtos family of Greek traditional dances. Performers begin by forming two lines arranged within a circle. At specific intervals indicated by the accompanying song, the dancers transition seamlessly from two lines into a single file line, later reforming back into two lines. This shifting spatial arrangement forms the core structural dynamic of the performance.

Costume and setting details are likewise not described in sources beyond its open-air and hall settings during the Apokries festivities on Samos. Occasions and meaning center on the festive period of Carnival and communal social gatherings, embodying regional identity through the literary link to Sideris Zisimou.
